original_question: Develop an algorithmic procedure that, given an ordinary differential equation with the Painleve property, decides whether the equation can be solved in terms of one of the Painleve equations or an associated Painleve sigma-equation.
target_in_paper: Open Problem 2.9 in Section 2, read together with the sharper introductory formulation in Section 1, item 1: the Painlevé equivalence problem.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s intended target. It correctly identifies that the problem is algorithmic, assumes the input equation has the Painlevé property, and asks for a decision as to whether the equation is solvable in terms of a canonical Painlevé object. It also correctly includes the associated Painlevé σ-form language from the introduction, so it stays aligned with the paper’s first listed open problem rather than drifting into unrelated numerical or classification questions.
missing_details: The paper explicitly names this as the Painlevé equivalence problem; that label is part of the intended scope.
The canonical targets are the six Painlevé equations PI–PVI, namely equations (1.1)–(1.6); the draft does not say that the procedure should identify which canonical equation occurs.
In the classical Painlevé–Gambier setting discussed nearby, the equation is a second-order first-degree ODE of the form w'' = F(w,w',z), where F is rational in w and w' and locally analytic in z.

For that classical setting, equivalence is considered up to a Möbius (bilinear rational) change of variables W(ζ) = (a(z)w + b(z))/(c(z)w + d(z)), ζ = φ(z); Section 2 specifically asks how one determines this transformation.
The σ-equations are not arbitrary auxiliary equations: they are the Hamiltonian second-order, second-degree Painlevé σ-equations SI–SVI associated with PI–PVI.

Section 2 separates off autonomous equations or equations with symmetries, which are expected to admit first integrals and hence be solvable by elliptic equations, linear equations, or quadratures; the intended equivalence problem is the remaining non-autonomous, symmetry-free case.

The paper’s official formulation is a recognition/equivalence question—how to know whether an ODE is Painlevé-solvable—not a request for a universal closed-form solver for every ODE with the Painlevé property.
refined_question: Develop algorithmic procedures for the Painlevé equivalence problem: given an ordinary differential equation with the Painlevé property—especially, in the classical setting, a second-order first-degree equation w'' = F(w,w',z) with F rational in w and w' and locally analytic in z—determine whether the equation can, after the appropriate admissible change of variables (classically a Möbius transformation W(ζ) = (a(z)w + b(z))/(c(z)w + d(z)), ζ = φ(z)), be reduced to one of the canonical Painlevé equations PI–PVI, or in Hamiltonian form to one of the associated Painlevé σ-equations SI–SVI; and, if so, identify the canonical target equation and the transformation.
justification: This draft targets the paper’s first open problem. The introduction states, in item 1 of the paper’s list of open problems, that one should develop algorithmic procedures for the Painlevé equivalence problem: given an equation with the Painlevé property, determine whether it is solvable in terms of a Painlevé equation or a Painlevé σ-equation. Section 2 then gives the nearest official standalone formulation as Open Problem 2.9, asking how one knows whether an ODE with the Painlevé property can be solved in terms of a Painlevé transcendent. The nearby context supplies the missing structure: the classical Painlevé–Gambier class is w'' = F(w,w',z) with F rational in w,w' and locally analytic in z, classified up to Möbius transformation; the σ-equations arise from the Hamiltonian formulation and are the associated second-order, second-degree equations. Because this paper has no Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3, the closest paper-faithful target is Open Problem 2.9 together with the introductory item 1.
